en: The Sūtra of the King of Medicine, Lapis Lazuli Light.
Oṃ, homage to the Omniscient One!
Homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour of the countryside, arrived in due course at the great city of Vaiśālī.
There, the Blessed One dwelt at Vaiśālī at the foot of the Vādyasvara tree together with a large community of monks.

Together with eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-six thousand bodhisattvas, surrounded and honored by an assembly of kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, he was teaching the Dharma.

Then Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, rising from his seat through the power of the Buddha, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "May the Blessed One teach the names of those Tathāgatas."

"Having heard the detailed analysis of their former vows, may we purify all karmic obscurations for the sake of benefiting sentient beings in the final age, in the final time, when the semblance of the True Dharma prevails.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
O Mañjuśrī, you are the one of great compassion;
having generated immeasurable compassion,
you exert yourself for the sake, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings obstructed by various karmic hindrances, and for the benefit of gods and humans.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; attend well and thoroughly to what I shall say.
"So be it, Blessed One," [he replied].
Thus Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him:
"Mañjuśrī, in the eastern direction, beyond as many Buddha-fields from this Buddha-field as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers, there is a world-system named Vaidūryanirbhāsā."

There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when that Blessed One Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he made these twelve great vows:
They existed.
What are the twelve great vows?
His first great vow was: "When, in a future time, I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,"
Then, by the radiance of my body, immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite world-systems would shine, glow, and blaze;
and just as I am endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
my body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics.
In the same way, may all sentient beings come to be.

His second great vow was this: "When, in a future time, I shall awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then, upon attaining awakening, my body shall be utterly pure within and without, endowed with stainless radiance like a priceless lapis lazuli gem;
and that vast body shall be manifest with corresponding glory and splendor."
The networks of its rays would surpass even the beams of the sun and moon; and whatever beings are born in this world-system,
as well as those men, should they travel in various directions during the darkness of the night, [they would see].
Touched by my radiance in all directions, may they perform virtuous deeds.
His third great vow was this:

"When, in the future— [omitted]— I have attained awakening, may those beings who, through the empowerment of immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, become [the cause] for the inexhaustible enjoyment and utilization of the infinite realm of sentient beings [be so]."
No sentient being shall suffer from any deficiency whatsoever.

His fourth great vow was: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may I establish those beings who have entered upon wrong paths—those who have entered the path of the śrāvakas and those who have entered the path of the pratyekabuddhas—in the unsurpassed path of awakening, the Mahāyāna."
His fifth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may all those beings who practice the holy life under my teaching possess unbroken morality and be well-restrained;
and may no one [violate it]."
If, having heard my name, one who has failed in ethical discipline should go to a state of woe anywhere, [may I not attain enlightenment].

His sixth great vow was this: "When, in the future—[at that time] when I have attained awakening—whatever beings there may be who have inferior bodies, impaired faculties, or ugly complexions; who are dull-witted, mute, or deformed; who are lame, hunchbacked, afflicted with leprosy, crippled, blind, deaf, or insane; and whatever other diseases may reside in their bodies,"
Upon hearing my name, may they all have their sense faculties restored and their bodies become perfectly complete.
His seventh great vow was this: "When, in the future— then, when I have attained awakening—
whatever beings are afflicted by various diseases, who are without protection, without refuge, deprived of medicines and requisites,
helpless, poor, and suffering— if..."
If my name should fall upon their ears,
may all their diseases be pacified,
and may they be free from illness and free from affliction until the very end of awakening.

His eighth great vow was this: "In the future, whenever any woman— desiring to be completely liberated from the female womb and from the state of womanhood, which is loathsome and afflicted by hundreds of various feminine defects— should hold my name in mind,"
That woman shall no longer possess the female state until she reaches the culmination of enlightenment.

His ninth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, I shall turn back all sentient beings who are bound by the fetters of Māra’s snares and have fallen into the perilous thickets of various views; having freed them from all the snares of Māra and all states of wrong view, I shall establish them in right view and gradually demonstrate to them the conduct of a bodhisattva."
His tenth great vow was this: "In the future, when I have attained awakening, may whatever sentient beings are terrified by the fear of kings and the like,

or those who are bound in fetters and imprisoned, or those deserving of death, or those afflicted by many calamities, or those who are insulted and struck by physical, verbal, and mental sufferings— may they all, upon hearing my name and through the power of my merit, be completely liberated from all fears and calamities."

His eleventh great vow was this: "When, in the future— then, when I have attained awakening— whatever sentient beings are inflamed by the fire of hunger and, being intent on seeking food and drink, commit evil deeds on that account,
if they should hold my name in mind,"
I would satisfy their bodies with food endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
His twelfth great vow was this: "When, in the future— [attaining enlightenment]— then, for whatever beings who are destitute of clothing, poor, and afflicted by cold, heat, gadflies, and mosquitoes,
and who experience suffering,
if they should hold my name in mind,"
I would provide them with the enjoyment of garments,
I would present them with sensual pleasures dyed in various colors,
and I would fulfill all the intentions of all sentient beings through various jewel ornaments, perfumes, garlands, ointments, musical instruments, cymbals, and vocal performances.
Mañjuśrī, these twelve great vows were made by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, while he was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, as for the vow of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, and as for the array of qualities of his buddha-field, it is not possible to exhaust them even in an eon or the remainder of an eon.
That buddha-field is utterly pure, free from stones, pebbles, and gravel; it is devoid of the faults of desire and free from the sound of suffering in the lower realms; it is without women.
And that great earth is made of lapis lazuli, with its walls, ramparts, palaces, archways, windows, lattices, and turrets composed of the seven precious gems, just like the world-system Sukhāvatī.
In that world-system Vaidūryanirbhāsā, there were two bodhisattva mahāsattvas who were the leaders of those immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva mahāsattvas: one was named Sūryavairocana,
and the second was Candravairocana.
Those who uphold the treasury of the true Dharma of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha—
for this reason, Mañjuśrī, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family should make a vow to be reborn in that buddha-field.
Furthermore, the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there are ordinary beings who do not know wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Overcome by greed and lacking understanding, they do not know giving or the great maturation of giving."
Foolish and ignorant, lacking the faculty of faith, they are preoccupied with the momentary accumulation of wealth;
their minds do not incline toward giving or sharing.
When the time for giving arrives, they experience mental suffering as if their own body or flesh were being cut away.
And there are many beings who do not even consume it themselves,
much less give it to their mothers, fathers, wives, or daughters,
much less to their male and female slaves or laborers.
How much more so for other supplicants!
Such beings, having passed away from here, will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts or in the animal realm.
However, those who, while previously existing as humans, have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, [shall not fall into such states].

There, for those dwelling in the world of Yama or dwelling in the animal realm, the name of that Tathāgata will appear before them. Merely by recollecting it, they will pass away from there and be reborn once again in the human world.
They will become rememberers of their past lives;
terrified by the fear of miserable rebirths, they will no longer seek the qualities of sensual pleasure,
but will delight in giving and speak in praise of generosity.
By means of total renunciation, they will gradually bestow their hands, feet, head, eyes, flesh, and blood upon supplicants,
let alone any other mass of wealth.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who, having undertaken the precepts for the sake of the Tathāgata, fall into a failure of morality,
or occasionally fall into a failure of view or a failure of conduct.
Furthermore, those who have failed in ethical discipline may become possessed of ethical discipline and guard their morality,
yet they do not seek out extensive learning.
And they do not understand the profound meaning spoken by the Tathāgata;
moreover, those who are learned will become conceited and stiff with pride.

Devoted to envy toward others, they despise and reject the true Dharma. Such deluded persons are partisans of Māra; having themselves entered upon a wrong path, they cause many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other beings to fall into a great abyss.
For those beings of such a kind, their destination will for the most part be residence in hell;
however, among them, those who have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, [will not fall there].
While they remain there in that hell, through the power of the Buddha, the name of that Tathāgata will become manifest to them.
Having passed away from there, they will be reborn once again in the human world, endowed with right view, energetic, virtuous, and upright.
Abandoning their homes, they will go forth into the religious life under the teaching of the Tathāgata and will gradually fulfill the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who speak in praise of themselves while being stingy,

and who utter dispraise of others; these beings, who exalt themselves and disparage others, having treated one another with contempt, will experience suffering in the three miserable realms for many thousands of years.
After the passing of many thousands of years, having died there, they are reborn among the animal wombs such as cattle, horses, camels, and donkeys.
Beaten by the striking of whips and sticks, their bodies tormented by hunger and thirst, they travel along the road carrying heavy burdens.
If, at some time, they should obtain a human birth,
They will always be reborn in low-born families and will remain under the control of others as slaves;
however, those who, while previously in human form, have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, [shall not suffer such things].
By that root of merit, they will be completely liberated from all sufferings;
they will possess sharp faculties and be wise, discerning, and intelligent. Devoted to the pursuit of the wholesome, they will constantly obtain the company of spiritual friends.
Having severed the snare of Māra, they shatter the eggshell of ignorance;
they dry up the river of afflictions and are completely liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, fear, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, there are beings who delight in slander and cause sentient beings to engage in mutual quarrels, strife, and disputes.
With minds intent on conflict toward one another, those beings perform various kinds of unwholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind;
desiring harm for each other, they constantly strive for the detriment of one another.
They invoke forest deities, tree deities, and mountain deities;
they invoke various spirits in cremation grounds;
and they deprive living beings belonging to the animal realm of their lives.
They worship yakṣas and rākṣasas who consume flesh and blood;

having fashioned either the name or a physical image of that enemy, they perform terrible incantations there, desiring to bring about an end to life or the destruction of the body through the application of *kākhorda* and *vetāla* spells.
However, for those who have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, [no such harm shall come].
It is impossible for anyone to create an obstacle for them;
they all dwell with mutual thoughts of loving-kindness, thoughts of benefit, and thoughts free from malice, content with their own respective possessions.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, these four assemblies— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—

and any other faithful sons of good family or daughters of good family who are endowed with the eightfold noble path and observe the fast, or who shall maintain the precepts for one year or for three months;
Those who have such a vow and such an intention— “By this root of merit, may we be reborn in the western direction, in the world-system Sukhāvatī, where the Tathāgata Amitāyus resides”—

and those who have heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, for them at the time of death, eight bodhisattvas will arrive by means of their supernatural power and appear before them.
There they will appear by spontaneous birth upon lotuses of various colors;
some, moreover, will be reborn in the world of the gods.
For those who have been reborn there, their former...
Their roots of merit will not be exhausted, nor will they go to an evil rebirth;
having passed away from there, they will be reborn here in the human world.
They will become kings, universal monarchs (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents;
they will establish many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Others, moreover, will be reborn in great kṣatriya families, in great brahmin families, and in families abundant in wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses.
They will be endowed with physical beauty,
they will be endowed with sovereignty,
and they will be endowed with a retinue.
And whatever woman, having heard the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, shall take it up, for her that very state of being female is to be expected as her last.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in the future time, in the final age, I shall cause those faithful sons of good family and daughters of good family to hear the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha."

I shall cause even the name of a Buddha to enter into the ears of those who will uphold, recite, teach, master, and extensively proclaim this jewel of a sūtra to others, even for as long as a single moment of sleep.
They will write it down or cause it to be written down;
or, having made it into a book, they will honor it with various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Having wrapped it in five-colored cloths, it should be placed in a clean location.
Wherever this sūtra is established,
there the four great kings with their retinues and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other deities will approach.

There this sutra shall circulate; and those, O Blessed One, shall proclaim this jewel of a sutra, and they shall uphold the name of that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha and the detailed exposition of the distinctions of that Tathāgata’s former special vows.
For them there will be no untimely death; no one will be able to steal away their vital energy (ojas),
and even if their vital energy has been stolen, they recover it once again.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī; it is just so, as you say."
And Mañjuśrī, whichever faithful son of good family or daughter of good family should desire to perform an offering to that Tathāgata, he should have an image of that Tathāgata made,
and for seven days and nights he should observe the fast endowed with the noble eightfold path.

Having prepared pure food with purity, in a clean place— strewn with various flowers, perfumed with various incenses, and adorned with various garments, umbrellas, banners, and flags— one whose limbs are well-washed, who wears pure and stainless clothing, and whose mind is stainless, untroubled, free from ill will, and possessed of a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings (and a mind of equanimity), [should proceed].
One should maintain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
While the sounds of various musical instruments and songs are being played, one should circumambulate that image of the Tathāgata, keep in mind the fulfilled vows of that Tathāgata,
and set forth this sūtra.
Whatever one intends and whatever one prays for, he fulfills every such aspiration.
If one desires long life,
one becomes long-lived;
if one prays for wealth, [one obtains it].
He becomes enriched with enjoyments;
if he prays for sovereignty,
he attains it with little difficulty.
If one desires a son,
one obtains a son;
those who see an evil dream here [shall likewise be freed from it].
Wherever a crow is perched as an ill omen,
or wherever hundreds of inauspicious things are present, one should perform worship to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.

All evil dreams, ill omens, and inauspicious conditions shall be pacified. Those who experience fear from weapons, water, poison, fire, or from fierce elephants, lions, tigers, bears, hyenas, leopards, venomous snakes, scorpions, centipedes, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like,
should perform worship to that Tathāgata.
They shall be liberated from all fears;
those who have fear of thieves or fear of bandits should perform worship to that Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, those faithful sons of good family or daughters of good family who take refuge in the Three Jewels for as long as they live,
who do not have other deities,
and who uphold the five precepts—
Those who maintain the bodhisattva vow consisting of four hundred excellent precepts,
and furthermore, those monks who have gone forth from the household life and maintain two hundred and fifty precepts;

Those bhikṣuṇīs who uphold the five hundred training rules, and those who have fallen away from any one of the training rules as they were undertaken— if they are terrified by the fear of miserable rebirths,
they should hold in mind the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
No further suffering from going to the three lower realms is to be expected for them.
Furthermore, whatever woman experiences intense, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations at the time of childbirth,
if she should recollect the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, [she shall be freed from it].
And she should perform worship;
thus she will give birth with ease to a son who is complete in all his limbs.
He will give birth to one who is handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold, with sharp faculties and great intelligence;
he will be healthy and free from much illness, and it will not be possible for non-human beings to steal away his vital energy.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you have faith and conviction in what I shall describe as the qualities of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha?"
"Or do you have any doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation regarding this profound sphere of the Buddha?
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, I have no doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation regarding these discourses spoken by the Tathāgata. Why is that?"
There is no lack of purity in the conduct of body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas.
Blessed One, even these two, the sun and the moon, so possessed of great supernatural power and great majesty, might fall to the earth;
or even Sumeru, the king of mountains, might move from its place.
But the word of the Buddhas cannot be otherwise. However, Venerable Sir, there are beings who lack the faculty of faith;
having heard of this sphere of the Buddhas, they will say: "How can there be such vast qualities and benefits from merely recollecting the name of that Tathāgata?"
They do not believe, they do not trust, and they reject it; for them, this will lead to misfortune, lack of welfare, lack of happiness, and downfall for a long time.
The Blessed One said: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question, that a sentient being who has heard the name of that Tathāgata should go to a state of woe or an evil rebirth."
This is not possible.
And, Ānanda, the range of the Buddhas is difficult to believe;
yet you, Ānanda, have faith and trust in it.

This should be seen as the power of the Tathāgata; this is not the domain of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, with the exception of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are bound to only one more birth. Ānanda, the attainment of a human birth is difficult to find.
Faith and reverence toward the Three Jewels are difficult to find;
hearing the name of the Tathāgata is even more difficult to find.
Ānanda, the bodhisattva conduct of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, is immeasurable.
His skill in means is also immeasurable,
and the detailed extent of his specific vows is immeasurable;
were I to desire it, I could [describe] that Tathāgata for an eon.
Or, Ānanda, were I to describe in detail and at length the remainder of the kalpas of the bodhisattva conduct,
it might come to an end,
but it is simply not possible to reach the end of the detailed account of the specific former vows of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
Now at that time, in that very assembly, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Trāṇamukta who was present and seated.

Rising from his seat, he draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Venerable Sir, there will be..."

"Blessed One, in the future time, in the final age, beings will be afflicted by various diseases; with their limbs wasted by chronic illness, their throats and lips parched by hunger and thirst, facing death, surrounded by weeping friends, kinsmen, and relatives, seeing the directions as darkness, and being dragged away by the messengers of Yama."
When his body lies upon the bier, his consciousness is led before Yama, the King of Dharma.
Whatever wholesome or unwholesome deeds have been committed by that person, which are naturally attached to him,
all of that is recorded in writing and presented to Yama, the King of Dharma.

Then Yama, the King of Dharma, also questions him and calculates his wholesome or unwholesome deeds exactly as they were performed, and issues a command accordingly. In that regard, those friends, kinsmen, and blood relatives of that sick person who take refuge in the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, for the sake of that patient—
If they were to perform worship to that Tathāgata,
it is possible that his consciousness might return once more,
such that he perceives himself as if he had entered back into a dream.
Whether on the seventh day, or the twenty-first day, or the thirty-fifth day, or the forty-ninth day, his consciousness may return once more, and he may regain mindfulness.
The ripening of his wholesome or unwholesome karma becomes directly manifest to him of its own accord.
Having known this, he will never again commit a sinful or unwholesome deed even for the sake of his life.
Therefore, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family should perform worship to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the bodhisattva Trāṇamukta: "Noble son, how should one perform the worship of that Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha?

The bodhisattva Trāṇamukta replied: "Venerable Ānanda, those who wish to liberate someone from a great illness should, for the sake of that sick person, observe the fast endowed with the eight noble limbs for seven days."
One should perform worship and service for the community of monks with food, drink, and all necessary requisites according to one's ability.
One should keep the name of the Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, in mind three times during the night and three times during the day.
This sutra should be recited forty-nine times.
Forty-nine lamps are to be lit.
Seven images are to be made;
for each image, seven lamps are to be lit.
Each lamp should be made the size of a cartwheel;
if the light does not diminish on the thirty-ninth day,
it should be known that all success has been attained.
Fifty-nine five-colored banners should be made.

Furthermore, Reverend Ānanda, for those consecrated Kṣatriya kings to whom calamities or portents may have arisen— whether affliction by disease, affliction by their own army, affliction by an enemy army, affliction by the stars, affliction by eclipses of the moon or sun, affliction by untimely wind and rain, or affliction by drought that has broken out—
Whether there be an inauspicious omen, a contagious disease, or a calamity that has arisen,
that anointed Kṣatriya king must maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings,
and he must release those beings who have been cast into bondage.

And for that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, the worship should be performed as previously described. Then, by this root of merit and through the detailed excellence of the former vows of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, there [shall be] for that consecrated Kṣatriya king...
The realm will be secure and well-supplied with food;
there will be timely winds, rains, and abundance of crops;
and all sentient beings dwelling in the realm will be healthy, happy, and full of joy.
Furthermore, in that realm, malevolent yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and piśācas will not harass sentient beings,
nor will they see any ill omens.
And for that anointed kṣatriya king, there will be an increase in lifespan, complexion, strength, health, and sovereignty.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the bodhisattva Trāṇamukta: "Noble son, how is it that one whose lifespan is completely exhausted increases it once again?
The bodhisattva Trāṇamukta replied: "Venerable Ānanda, have you not heard from the Tathāgata himself that there are untimely deaths?
To avert those, the application of mantras and medicinal herbs has been taught."
There are beings who are afflicted by illness,
yet their illness is not severe; however, they lack medicine and an attendant,
or perhaps physicians do not provide the medicine.
This is the first untimely death.
The second untimely death is that of one who meets their end by the punishment of the king.
The third untimely death is that of those who are excessively heedless and dwell in negligence.
Humans steal their vital energy (*ojas*).
The fourth untimely death is those who pass away by being consumed by fire;
the fifth untimely death is those who die by water.
The sixth untimely death is that of those who dwell among lions, tigers, serpents, and fierce wild beasts, and die therein;
the seventh untimely death is that of those who fall from mountain precipices.
The eighth untimely death is that of those who die through the employment of poisons, *kākhorda* spells, and *vetāla* rites.
The ninth untimely death is that of those who, afflicted by hunger and thirst and unable to obtain food or drink, pass away in agony.
These, in brief, are the untimely deaths taught by the Tathāgata.
And there are other immeasurable untimely deaths as well.
Then, indeed, twelve great yakṣa generals were assembled there in that assembly; namely, the great yakṣa general named Kiṃbhīra, the great yakṣa general named Vajra,
and the great yakṣa general named Mekhila.
The great yakṣa general named Anila, the great yakṣa general named Anila, and the great yakṣa general named Saṇṭhila.
The great yakṣa general named Indala,
the great yakṣa general named Pāyila, and the great yakṣa general named Mahāla.
The great yakṣa general named Cidāla,
the great yakṣa general named Caundhula,
and the great yakṣa general named Vikala.

These twelve great yakṣa generals, each surrounded by their own retinues of followers, spoke thus with one voice to the Blessed One: "We have heard, through the power of the Buddha, the name of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha."
We no longer have fear of the miserable realms.
Therefore, united and in harmony, for as long as we live, we go for refuge to the Buddha;
we go for refuge to the Dharma.
We go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
For the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, we shall exert ourselves;
especially [for those] in a village or...
Whether in a city, a village, or a forest hermitage, whoever shall propagate this sutra,
or whoever shall uphold the name of that Blessed One, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, and perform worship and service to him;
We shall protect that being, we shall preserve it,
and we shall liberate it from all inauspiciousness.
"We shall fulfill all their hopes.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to those yakṣa generals, saying: "Excellent, excellent, great yakṣa generals!
It is well that you, remembering your gratitude toward the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, have set out for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse? And how should I remember it?
The Blessed One said: “In that case, Ānanda, remember this Dharma discourse as ‘The Detailed Account of the Particular Former Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.’”
"Remember this as 'The Vow of the Twelve Great Yakṣa Generals.'"
Thus spoke the Blessed One;
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and the Venerable Ānanda were uplifted in mind.
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta,
those Bodhisattvas,
and those Great Śrāvakas.
And those kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders,
the entire assembly,
and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra entitled "The King of Lapis Lazuli Radiance, the Medicine Guru."
